(a) **decreases**. For a conservative force \(\Delta V = -W\), so positive work done by the force lowers the potential energy (a falling body loses potential energy as gravity does positive work on it).

(b) **kinetic** energy. Friction converts the body's energy of motion into heat; potential energy depends only on position and is untouched by friction.

(c) **external force**. By Newton's Third Law the internal forces cancel in pairs, so \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{P}/\mathrm{d}t = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}\).

(d) **total linear momentum** and **total energy**. Momentum is conserved in every collision, and energy is conserved once all forms are counted; it is the total KINETIC energy that changes, which is what makes the collision inelastic.

(a) **False.** In an elastic collision it is the TOTAL momentum and TOTAL kinetic energy of the system that are conserved, not those of each body separately — each body's momentum and kinetic energy generally change (that is the whole point of a collision).

(b) **False.** Total energy is conserved only for an isolated system. If external forces act and do work on the system, they add or remove energy, so the system's total energy changes.

(c) **False.** The work over a closed loop is zero only for CONSERVATIVE forces. Friction and other dissipative forces do negative work on every leg of the path, so their work over a closed loop is non-zero.

(d) **False**, because of the word 'always'. In the usual inelastic collision part of the kinetic energy does go into deformation, heat and sound, so the final kinetic energy is indeed less. But an inelastic collision is defined only by kinetic energy NOT being conserved, and that includes the case where stored internal energy is RELEASED during the collision — two trolleys latched together by a compressed spring that unlatches on impact, or an explosive collision. There the final kinetic energy exceeds the initial. So the statement is usually true but not universally true, and 'always' makes it false.

(a) **No.** While the balls are in contact they are deformed, and part of the kinetic energy is momentarily stored as elastic potential energy of deformation. Kinetic energy is conserved only when compared BEFORE and AFTER the collision; during the contact it is not.

(b) **Yes.** The forces the two balls exert on each other are equal and opposite at every instant (Newton's Third Law), so the impulses cancel and the total linear momentum is conserved at every instant of the collision. External forces such as gravity are negligible over the very short contact time.

(c) For an inelastic collision the answer to (b) is unchanged — total linear momentum is still conserved, during and after. The answer to (a) is also 'no', and here the kinetic energy is not recovered afterwards either: some of it is permanently converted into heat, sound and deformation.

(d) **Elastic.** A potential energy that depends only on the separation of the centres corresponds to a conservative force. Energy stored during compression is fully returned during recovery, so no kinetic energy is lost overall.

**Momentum:** Yes, momentum IS conserved — but only for the system as a whole. The molecule's own momentum changes: taking the normal to the wall as the \(x\)-axis, the normal component reverses from \(+mv\cos 30^{\circ}\) to \(-mv\cos 30^{\circ}\), a change of magnitude

\(|\Delta p| = 2mv\cos 30^{\circ} = 2m(200)\cos 30^{\circ} = 346\,m\;\text{(SI units)}\)

while the component parallel to the wall is unchanged. That lost momentum is not destroyed — it is transferred to the wall (and hence to the container), so the total momentum of molecule + wall is conserved. Momentum is conserved in every collision.

**Elastic or inelastic:** The molecule rebounds with the SAME speed, so \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\) is unchanged and no kinetic energy is lost. The collision is therefore **elastic**.

Answer: momentum is conserved (for the molecule-plus-wall system); the collision is elastic.

Take \(g = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) and the density of water as \(10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\).

Mass of water raised: \(m = 30\,\text{m}^3\times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3} = 3\times 10^{4}\,\text{kg}\)

Useful work done against gravity:

\(W = mgh = 3\times 10^{4}\times 9.8\times 40 = 1.176\times 10^{7}\,\text{J}\)

Time \(t = 15\,\text{min} = 900\,\text{s}\), so the useful (output) power is

\(P_{\text{out}} = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{1.176\times 10^{7}}{900} = 1.31\times 10^{4}\,\text{W}\)

The pump is only \(30\%\) efficient, so the electric power drawn is

\(P_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{P_{\text{out}}}{0.30} = \dfrac{1.31\times 10^{4}}{0.30} = 4.36\times 10^{4}\,\text{W}\)

Answer: \(P \approx 4.36\times 10^{4}\,\text{W} \approx 43.6\,\text{kW}\).

An elastic collision must satisfy BOTH conservation of linear momentum and conservation of kinetic energy. Before the collision, with each ball of mass \(m\), the momentum is \(mV\) and the kinetic energy is \(\frac{1}{2}mV^2\). Test each outcome.

First outcome (ball 1 at rest, balls 2 and 3 moving together at \(V/2\)):
momentum \(= 2m(V/2) = mV\) — conserved; kinetic energy \(= 2\times\frac{1}{2}m(V/2)^2 = \frac{1}{4}mV^2\), which is only HALF of \(\frac{1}{2}mV^2\). Kinetic energy is not conserved, so this is not possible.

Second outcome (balls 1 and 2 at rest, ball 3 moving at \(V\)):
momentum \(= mV\) — conserved; kinetic energy \(= \frac{1}{2}mV^2\) — conserved. Both conditions hold, so this IS possible.

Third outcome (all three moving together at \(V/3\)):
momentum \(= 3m(V/3) = mV\) — conserved; kinetic energy \(= 3\times\frac{1}{2}m(V/3)^2 = \frac{1}{6}mV^2\), only a third of the initial value. Not possible.

Note that all three outcomes conserve momentum — it is the kinetic-energy condition that selects the answer, which is why momentum alone is never enough to settle an elastic collision.

Answer: only the second outcome, in which balls 1 and 2 come to rest and ball 3 moves off with speed \(V\), is possible.

For a head-on ELASTIC collision between two bodies of EQUAL mass, with the target at rest, Eqs. (5.26) and (5.27) give

\(v_{1f} = \left(\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)v_{1i} = 0\) and \(v_{2f} = \dfrac{2m_1 v_{1i}}{m_1 + m_2} = v_{1i}\)

That is, the incoming bob stops dead and hands its entire velocity to the stationary bob.

So bob A arrives at the bottom with speed \(v = \sqrt{2gL(1 - \cos 30^{\circ})}\), transfers all of it to bob B, and is left at rest at the lowest point. With zero kinetic energy after the collision it cannot climb at all.

Answer: bob A does not rise — it rises to a height of ZERO, and bob B moves off with the speed A had just before impact.

Take \(g = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). Released from the horizontal, the bob falls through a height equal to the length of the pendulum, \(h = L = 1.5\,\text{m}\).

Initial potential energy relative to the lowest point: \(mgL\)

Of this, \(5\%\) is dissipated against air resistance, so \(95\%\) survives as kinetic energy at the lowest point:

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0.95\,mgL\)

The mass cancels, which is why it is not needed:

\(v = \sqrt{2\times 0.95\times g\times L} = \sqrt{2\times 0.95\times 9.8\times 1.5} = \sqrt{27.93}\)

\(v = 5.28\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Answer: \(v \approx 5.3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

The sand leaks out through a hole in the FLOOR, so it leaves the trolley moving vertically downward relative to the trolley — it carries away exactly the horizontal velocity it already had, and it is not thrown backwards or forwards.

Consequently the leaking sand exerts no horizontal thrust on the trolley, and the track is frictionless, so there is NO horizontal external force on the trolley at any stage. Applying conservation of horizontal momentum to the trolley alone: its mass decreases, but so does its momentum in exactly the same proportion, leaving its velocity unchanged.

(Contrast this with a rocket, where the exhaust is expelled backwards at high speed relative to the vehicle and therefore does accelerate it.)

The leak rate of \(0.05\,\text{kg s}^{-1}\) and the sandbag mass of \(25\,\text{kg}\) fix only how long the leaking takes (\(500\,\text{s}\)); they do not affect the speed.

Answer: the speed is unchanged at \(27\,\text{km/h}\).

By the work-energy theorem, the work done by the NET force equals the change in kinetic energy, so no integration of the force is needed — only the speeds at the two ends.

At \(x = 0\): \(v_i = a(0)^{3/2} = 0\)

At \(x = 2\,\text{m}\): \(v_f = a(2)^{3/2} = 5\times 2\sqrt{2} = 14.14\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), so \(v_f^2 = 25\times 8 = 200\,\text{m}^2\,\text{s}^{-2}\)

Hence

\(W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}m(v_f^2 - v_i^2) = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 0.5\times 200 = 50\,\text{J}\)

Answer: \(W = 50\,\text{J}\).

(a) In time \(t\) the wind sweeps out a cylinder of cross-section \(A\) and length \(vt\), so the volume is \(Avt\) and the mass of air passing through is

\(m = \rho A v t\)

(b) That air moves with speed \(v\), so its kinetic energy is

\(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho A v^3 t\)

(c) The wind power available is the kinetic energy per unit time, \(\dfrac{1}{2}\rho A v^3\). With \(v = 36\,\text{km/h} = 10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(A = 30\,\text{m}^2\) and \(\rho = 1.2\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\):

\(P_{\text{wind}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 1.2\times 30\times (10)^3 = 1.8\times 10^{4}\,\text{W}\)

Only \(25\%\) is converted, so the electrical power produced is

\(P = 0.25\times 1.8\times 10^{4} = 4.5\times 10^{3}\,\text{W}\)

Answer: (a) \(m = \rho A v t\); (b) \(K = \frac{1}{2}\rho A v^3 t\); (c) \(P = 4.5\times 10^{3}\,\text{W} = 4.5\,\text{kW}\).

Take \(g = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

(a) Each lift raises \(10\,\text{kg}\) through \(0.5\,\text{m}\), so the work done against gravity per lift is \(mgh\), and for \(1000\) lifts

\(W = n\,mgh = 1000\times 10\times 9.8\times 0.5 = 4.9\times 10^{4}\,\text{J}\)

(The energy given back on lowering is stated to be dissipated, so it cannot be reused and does not reduce this figure.)

(b) Fat releases \(3.8\times 10^{7}\,\text{J}\) per kilogram, but only \(20\%\) becomes mechanical work:

usable energy per kilogram \(= 0.20\times 3.8\times 10^{7} = 7.6\times 10^{6}\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\)

Mass of fat used up:

\(m_{\text{fat}} = \dfrac{4.9\times 10^{4}}{7.6\times 10^{6}} = 6.45\times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}\)

Answer: (a) \(4.9\times 10^{4}\,\text{J}\); (b) \(6.45\times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}\), i.e. about \(6.45\,\text{g}\) of fat.

(a) Of the \(200\,\text{W}\) falling on each square metre, only \(20\%\) becomes useful electrical power:

useful power per unit area \(= 0.20\times 200 = 40\,\text{W m}^{-2}\)

To supply \(8\,\text{kW} = 8000\,\text{W}\) the required area is

\(A = \dfrac{8000}{40} = 200\,\text{m}^2\)

(b) \(200\,\text{m}^2\) is a square of side \(\sqrt{200} \approx 14\,\text{m}\). That is comparable to — indeed roughly the same as — the roof area of a typical house, so a family's entire power demand could in principle be met by covering its roof with solar collectors of this efficiency.

Answer: (a) \(A = 200\,\text{m}^2\); (b) comparable to the roof of a typical house (about \(14\,\text{m}\times 14\,\text{m}\)).
